title: The Holy Spirit in Preaching: Absolute Dependence on the Celestial Wind
seoTitle: The Holy Spirit in Preaching | Charles Spurgeon

content.text: The Absolute Inability of Human Persuasion

For Charles Haddon Spurgeon, the most flawless exposition of biblical doctrine and the most passionate evangelistic appeal were utterly powerless to save a single soul without the direct, supernatural intervention of the Holy Spirit. Despite being universally hailed as a master orator and the greatest preacher of his era, Spurgeon deeply understood the absolute spiritual inability of fallen humanity. In his landmark 1857 sermon on Regeneration, he emphatically declared that while a man may reform his outward behavior and conquer evil habits, "no man in the world can make himself to be born of God".

Spurgeon firmly believed that attempting to save a soul through mere human rhetoric was as foolish as standing over a corpse and commanding it to walk or stretch out its hand. The new birth, he argued, requires a divine interposition—an invincible, life-giving operation by the Holy Spirit. As he taught his congregation, "unless God the Holy Spirit, who 'worketh in us to will and to do,' should operate upon the will and the conscience, regeneration is an absolute impossibility".

This robust theological conviction shaped his entire homiletical method and his instruction to the next generation of ministers. In his Lectures to My Students, the "Prince of Preachers" solemnly warned his pastoral candidates against relying on their intellectual or communicative gifts. He urged them to cultivate all fields of knowledge and perfect themselves in oratory, but to simultaneously remember that "it is not by might, nor by power, that men are regenerated or sanctified, but 'by my Spirit, saith the Lord'".

Spurgeon compared an unanointed preacher to a mere musician playing a goodly instrument with a clear voice; such a man may reach the ear and entertain the intellect, but he will completely fail to touch the heart. True spiritual power, which depends entirely on the sovereign movement of the Holy Spirit—like a celestial wind blowing where it wishes—was the only force capable of turning a congregation of dead sinners into a congregation of living believers.

Because of this absolute dependence on the Holy Spirit, Spurgeon despised any attempt to artificially manufacture spiritual fervor or emotional manipulation in the pulpit. He instructed his students never to imitate the groans, shrieks, or dramatic pauses of other preachers merely to appear zealous. He stated plainly that "simulated ardor is a shameful form of lying". Instead of relying on theatrical tricks, the preacher must come fresh from the closet of private communion with God, clothed with the power of the Spirit, and speak to men with genuine, God-given unction.

For Spurgeon, the Holy Spirit was not a mere theoretical point of Reformed systematic theology; He was a present, living, and indispensable Agent in every single worship service. When a minister relies upon this supernatural power, the majesty of the truth compels men to listen. It was this total and humble reliance on the Spirit's quickening power that anchored Spurgeon's aggressive evangelism, allowing him to boldly command sinners to repent while knowing that only the breath of heaven could bring the dead to life.
